strengths: The paper proposes a clear and useful formulation for latent KV-cache compaction: matching both local attention outputs and unnormalized attention mass. The mass-matching argument via the mixture decomposition is technically persuasive and explains why per-token scalar biases are needed when compacting a block that will later be concatenated with fixed or future tokens.

The method is practically attractive. Once compact keys are selected, fitting biases with nonnegative least squares and values with least squares is simple, fast, and avoids the costly end-to-end optimization used by Cartridges. The paper also offers a sensible family of speed-quality tradeoffs, including OMP, accelerated OMP, and highest-attention variants.

The empirical evaluation is broader than many KV-compression papers: it covers three model families, QuALITY and LongHealth, multiple compaction ratios, token-pruning baselines, summarization, and Cartridges. The reported gains are meaningful, especially at high compaction ratios where the method often approaches or exceeds Cartridges while being much faster.

The ablations are useful and support the main design choices: biases, learned values, nonuniform head budgets, self-study/repeat-prefill reference queries, and on-policy queries. The appendices provide substantial implementation detail, including baseline adaptations, query generation, numerical solvers, chunked compaction, and OMP speedups.

The work is significant for long-context inference systems because it studies a reusable primitive, one-shot KV compaction, rather than only online eviction. The approach appears compatible with existing inference systems in principle and could complement retrieval or summarization.
weaknesses: The evaluation, while promising, has limited statistical grounding. QuALITY uses the first 50 validation contexts rather than a randomized or full evaluation, Cartridges is evaluated only on a 20-context subset and only for Qwen, and LongHealth has only 4 concatenated contexts. The paper mostly reports curves without confidence intervals or significance tests, making some close comparisons hard to interpret.

The Cartridges comparison is important but not fully satisfying. The authors use default repository settings and acknowledge that more optimization or different self-study data may improve Cartridges. Since the headline claim emphasizes matching or beating Cartridges at far lower cost, a more carefully tuned or compute-controlled comparison would strengthen the evidence.

Several baselines are adapted into a one-shot, question-agnostic setting, including SnapKV and PyramidKV, which changes their intended use. This is reasonable for the paper’s problem formulation, but the presentation should more clearly separate “best method for this deployment setting” from broader claims about outperforming prior KV-compression methods.

The systems claims are partly prospective. The method assumes support for scalar attention biases and benefits from variable-length per-head/nonuniform cache packing, but the paper does not demonstrate an integrated inference-engine implementation with end-to-end memory, latency, and throughput measurements during real serving. Wall-clock compaction time is reported, but downstream decode-time effects and implementation overheads are less established.

The core algorithm still relies on reference-query quality and subset selection for compact keys. The paper gives empirical evidence that self-study/repeat-prefill works, but there is little characterization of failure modes under distribution shift, multi-turn dialogue, tool-use contexts, or future queries that differ sharply from the reference queries.

Presentation is generally strong, but some figures are dense and hard to read, especially Figure 10 with long method names. More numeric tables for the main results would improve interpretability and reproducibility. The reproducibility package is not described; algorithms and hyperparameters are detailed, but code availability, seeds, exact prompts/settings, and hardware/software versions should be stated more explicitly.

Ethics and limitations are only lightly addressed. The LongHealth experiments involve clinical-style records, so the paper should more explicitly discuss privacy/sensitivity considerations and whether the benchmark is synthetic or de-identified, even if no new data are collected. The limitations section is honest about speed and extreme compaction, but less detailed on deployment risks such as silent loss of rare facts after compaction.

strengths: The paper targets an important systems/ML problem: reducing long-context KV-cache memory while preserving downstream behavior. The motivation is clear, and the distinction between physical cache size and logical sequence length is practically relevant for deployed long-context LMs.

The attention-matching formulation is intuitive and technically appealing. Matching both local attention outputs and unnormalized attention mass gives a clear reason for the learned scalar biases, and the decomposition into NNLS/least-squares subproblems is a useful way to avoid expensive per-context gradient optimization.

The empirical scope is broader than a minimal proof of concept: the authors evaluate on QuALITY and LongHealth, across Qwen3-4B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and Gemma-3-12B, and compare against summarization, Cartridges, H2O-style pruning, SnapKV, PyramidKV, and KVzip variants.

The paper includes several meaningful ablations, including biases, learned values, nonuniform head budgets, self-study queries, and on-policy queries. These help establish that the method is more than just highest-attention token selection.

The limitations section is relatively honest about important shortcomings: OMP+self-study can still take minutes, Cartridges can outperform at extreme 100x compaction on LongHealth, and the subset-selection restriction may limit quality.
weaknesses: The central empirical case is not strong enough for the breadth of the claims. QuALITY uses only the first 50 validation articles, and LongHealth uses only 4 concatenated contexts. This is a small basis for claims about robust long-context compaction across tasks and deployments, especially because LongHealth is the main 60k-token setting.

The comparison to Cartridges is incomplete and potentially unfair. Cartridges is evaluated only on Qwen for a 20-context QuALITY subset, and the authors explicitly use default settings while noting that additional or optimized Cartridges training may improve results. Since Cartridges is a major reference point for the paper's claimed speed-quality advantage, this weakens the main conclusion.

Several baselines are adapted into a question-agnostic one-shot setting that differs from their intended use, e.g. SnapKV and PyramidKV are made question-agnostic via a mock question. This is understandable for the target setting, but the paper sometimes presents the comparisons as broadly outperforming prior approaches rather than carefully qualifying them as comparisons under this modified protocol.

The strongest methods rely on substantial per-context query generation: self-study plus repeat-prefill, up to 50,000 reference queries per KV head, and around 5k self-study plus 7k repeat-prefill tokens per QuALITY context. This complicates the practical speed claims, and the reported timings are limited rather than a full end-to-end throughput/memory/latency analysis in an inference engine.

The method depends on attention implementations supporting per-token scalar biases and, for nonuniform compaction, efficient variable-length per-head KV packing. The paper argues these are supported in some kernels, but does not demonstrate an integrated deployment or quantify overheads under realistic serving workloads.

The theoretical justification is only a sufficient local argument over reference queries. The paper does not provide strong evidence that matching attention behavior on the sampled query distribution generalizes to arbitrary future user queries or generated trajectories, even though this is central to the compaction use case.

The nonuniform head-budget story is under-supported. The claim that head sensitivity is stable and transferable is based on limited curves and selected contexts, and the greedy allocation assumes approximate separability across heads without substantial validation.

Presentation of results relies heavily on plots with limited numeric reporting. Confidence intervals or statistical tests are mostly absent, making it difficult to judge whether differences between AM variants, KVzip, summarization, and Cartridges are reliable rather than noise from small evaluation sets.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The appendices provide useful implementation details, prompts, and baseline configurations, but the manuscript does not clearly commit to code release, exact seeds, all decoding settings beyond defaults, full hyperparameter choices for every plotted method, or raw per-task numerical results.

The paper has no meaningful research ethics or broader impacts discussion. There are no obvious severe ethical concerns, but the work targets memory and deployment infrastructure for LMs, where cost, privacy of retained latent state, and downstream misuse implications deserve at least brief treatment.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and technically well-motivated formulation for latent KV-cache compaction: matching both local attention outputs and unnormalized attention mass. The mass decomposition under concatenated KV blocks gives a convincing rationale for why learned scalar biases are needed and why the compacted cache should remain compatible with future tokens.

The method is practically attractive. Once compact keys are selected, fitting biases via NNLS and values via least squares is simple, efficient, and avoids expensive end-to-end optimization. The resulting family of methods gives useful speed-quality tradeoffs, including fast variants based on highest-attention key selection and accelerated OMP.

Empirical results are strong across several settings. On QuALITY and LongHealth, with Qwen3-4B, Llama-3.1-8B, and Gemma-3-12B, Attention Matching generally outperforms token-pruning and summarization baselines, and is competitive with or better than Cartridges at important high-compaction regimes while being much faster.

The ablations are informative: the paper separately studies learned biases, learned values, nonuniform head budgets, query generation, and on-policy queries. This makes the contribution more convincing than a single end-to-end benchmark comparison.

The paper is well written and reproducibility is above average at the manuscript level. It provides algorithmic details, solver choices, query-generation prompts, baseline configurations, timing breakdowns, and dataset/model details. The limitations section is honest about the remaining cost of OMP/self-study and about Cartridges sometimes doing better at extreme compression.
weaknesses: The evaluation is still narrower than the breadth of the claims suggests. QuALITY uses only 50 validation articles, Cartridges is evaluated only on a 20-context Qwen subset because of cost, and LongHealth uses only 4 constructed contexts. The trends are compelling, but statistical confidence and robustness across domains remain limited.

The systems implications are not fully demonstrated. The paper argues for practical deployment benefits, nonuniform per-head caches, scalar attention biases, and variable-length packing, but does not show an integrated inference-engine implementation with end-to-end throughput, memory, batching, and latency measurements under realistic serving workloads.

Several baselines require adaptation to the paper's one-shot, question-agnostic setting, especially SnapKV and PyramidKV. These adaptations are described, but they may not represent each baseline under its strongest intended use case, so some comparative conclusions should be interpreted carefully.

The strongest AM variants still require nontrivial context-specific computation, including self-study generation and OMP; Table 1 shows OMP can take hundreds of seconds for a 60k-token context. The fast variants help, but the practical break-even point versus cheaper summarization/pruning or simply using longer-context serving is not fully analyzed.

The method relies on reference queries being representative of future use. The paper studies several query sources and on-policy extraction, but there is limited stress testing for distribution shift, adversarial future queries, multi-turn interactive settings, or tasks where the post-compaction query distribution differs substantially from self-study/repeat-prefill.

The nonuniform budget procedure assumes approximate separability across heads and uses precomputed sensitivity curves. The evidence for stability is promising, but the approximation is not deeply validated, and it is unclear how often budgets must be recomputed across model variants, finetunes, domains, or context lengths.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and useful formulation of KV-cache compaction as attention-output plus attention-mass matching. The decomposition into key selection, NNLS bias fitting, and least-squares value fitting is technically well motivated, and the scalar-bias argument is especially compelling because it explains a systematic failure mode of ordinary token dropping under future concatenation.

The empirical results are strong across several settings. Attention Matching improves over token pruning/merging and summarization baselines on QuALITY, LongHealth, QASPER, LongBench v2, and RULER, and the reported speed/quality tradeoff versus Cartridges is practically significant.

The paper includes meaningful ablations: biases, learned values, nonuniform head budgets, query source, on-policy queries, aggregation choices, reconstruction loss, and online compaction. These support the claim that the gains come from the proposed components rather than a single benchmark artifact.

Presentation is generally clear. The method section gives enough mathematical detail to understand why mass preservation matters, and the appendices provide useful implementation details for OMP speedups, NNLS, chunking, and self-study query generation.

The limitations discussion is honest: the authors acknowledge that OMP+self-study can still take minutes, that Cartridges can outperform at more extreme 100x compression on some benchmarks, and that implementation in production inference engines requires additional systems work.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is not fully established from the manuscript alone. The paper gives detailed algorithms and hyperparameters, but does not indicate code release, exact random seeds, hardware/software versions beyond GPU type in places, or enough low-level integration detail to reproduce modified attention with per-token biases and nonuniform per-head cache packing in standard serving stacks.

Some comparisons are potentially fragile. Cartridges is evaluated only on Qwen and only on a 20-context QuALITY subset due to cost, while the subset has higher original-cache accuracy than the full set. The authors also note that additional Cartridges training may improve results, so the headline comparison to Cartridges is suggestive but not definitive.

Several baseline adaptations change the original setting of prior methods. SnapKV and PyramidKV are originally question-aware but are converted to question-agnostic mock-question variants; DuoAttention is attempted but omitted from the main results after poor performance. This is reasonable for the authors' target setting, but it weakens conclusions about superiority over those methods in their intended regimes.

The LongBench v2 protocol selects only 47 contexts where full-context succeeds and no-context fails. This isolates context-dependent examples, but the small, selected subset and stochastic decoding make the reported accuracies noisy and less representative of broad benchmark performance.

The method still has deployment caveats. It assumes access to internal KV/query activations, modified attention bias support, logical-position handling, and efficient variable-length/nonuniform head storage. The paper argues these are feasible, but does not demonstrate an end-to-end serving-system integration or measure user-facing latency/memory savings under realistic multi-request workloads.

The evaluation is broad but still mostly at small-to-mid model scales up to 12B dense models, with larger MoE scaling argued from KV-size considerations rather than empirically shown. Claims about scaling to deployed frontier-like systems therefore remain plausible but not directly validated.

Uncertainty estimates and statistical significance are limited. Many plots/tables report point estimates, sometimes on small numbers of contexts, and it is hard to judge robustness of close differences between AM variants, KVzip, and Cartridges at certain ratios.

strengths: The paper identifies an important practical problem: compacting KV caches for long-context inference without per-context gradient training. The proposed attention-matching formulation is conceptually clean, decomposing preservation under future concatenation into local attention-output matching plus unnormalized attention-mass matching.

The method is technically plausible and mostly well motivated. The per-token bias term is a useful insight for correcting systematic underestimation of compacted-prefix attention mass, and the least-squares/NNLS value and bias fitting gives a simple non-gradient implementation.

The empirical scope is broader than a single toy setting: results cover QuALITY, LongHealth, QASPER, LongBench v2, and RULER across Qwen, Llama, and Gemma variants, with comparisons to token eviction, token merging, summarization, KVzip, and Cartridges.

The appendices provide substantial implementation detail, including query generation, chunking, NNLS, OMP speedups, baseline configurations, and ablations. The limitations section is honest about runtime, extreme compaction failures, and systems integration needs.
weaknesses: The central empirical claims are not as convincing as the presentation suggests. The main QuALITY evaluation uses only 50 contexts, LongHealth uses only 4 concatenated contexts, and Cartridges is evaluated only on Qwen and only on a 20-context subset whose original-cache accuracy is higher than the full set. This makes the strongest comparative claims fragile.

The comparison to Cartridges is particularly underdetermined. The paper acknowledges that Cartridges may improve with more training or better self-study, while using default settings and limited runs. Since Cartridges is the key latent-space baseline, the claim of matching or exceeding it is not fully established.

Several baseline adaptations may disadvantage prior methods. SnapKV and PyramidKV are originally question-aware but are converted to a question-agnostic mock-question setup; DuoAttention is omitted after poor performance; leaderboard RULER numbers are mixed with the authors' own runs. These choices are explained, but they weaken the evidential force of the comparisons.

The evaluation lacks statistical rigor. Most reported downstream results have no confidence intervals, significance tests, or variance across random seeds, despite stochastic decoding and small sample counts in some settings. The LongBench v2 subset is selected based on full-context/no-context behavior, which is useful diagnostically but not an unbiased benchmark result.

The method may require nontrivial serving-stack changes: per-token attention biases, logical length distinct from physical cache length, variable-length per-head packing for nonuniform compaction, and careful RoPE handling. The paper argues compatibility, but does not demonstrate an integrated inference-engine implementation or end-to-end throughput/memory measurements.

Reproducibility is only moderate. Algorithmic details are extensive, but I did not see a code release or enough information to reproduce all engineering choices exactly, including model versions, decoding randomness, hardware-specific timings, and the nonuniform budget precomputation pipeline.

The paper gives limited treatment of risks and ethics. Since the method is aimed at preserving long-context memory, especially in agentic and medical-record-like settings, the discussion should more directly address privacy retention, stale or selectively lost context, instruction/safety degradation, and how failures would be detected in deployment.

Overall, the work is promising and likely useful, but the evidence overstates robustness and comparative superiority. I would lean weak accept because the core idea is sound and significant, while expecting stronger evaluation and reproducibility before relying on the claims operationally.

strengths: The paper addresses an important bottleneck in long-context LLM serving: reducing KV-cache size while preserving downstream behavior. The proposed attention matching objective is well motivated by the decomposition of attention over concatenated blocks into local attention outputs and attention mass, and the use of scalar per-token biases is a technically clean way to avoid systematic underestimation of compacted-prefix mass.

The method is practically appealing. Once compact keys are selected, fitting the mass weights via NNLS and compacted values via least squares gives a simple, largely closed-form procedure that avoids per-context end-to-end gradient optimization. This is a meaningful improvement over Cartridges-style latent cache optimization in settings where compaction latency matters.

The empirical evaluation is broad and convincing overall: QuALITY, LongHealth, QASPER, LongBench v2, and RULER; multiple model families including Qwen3, Llama-3.1, and Gemma-3; comparisons against summarization, token eviction/selection, token merging, KVzip, and Cartridges where feasible. The results consistently show strong performance in the high-compaction regime, often preserving near-full-context accuracy at 20x-100x compaction.

The paper includes useful ablations and analysis. It separately studies query sources, attention biases, value refitting, nonuniform head budgets, on-policy queries, aggregation rules, reconstruction loss versus downstream accuracy, and online compaction. These analyses support the central design choices rather than merely reporting headline benchmark gains.

The presentation is clear. The paper explains the objective, algorithms, implementation details, and experimental protocol carefully, and the limitations section is honest about remaining costs, 100x regimes where Cartridges can be stronger, and systems integration challenges.
weaknesses: Some central empirical comparisons are limited by computational constraints. Cartridges is evaluated only for Qwen on a 20-context QuALITY subset, and not across the full benchmark/model suite. Since Cartridges is the closest latent-space baseline, this leaves some uncertainty about the claimed quality comparison beyond the settings tested.

Several baseline adaptations may not fully represent the strongest possible versions of prior methods. SnapKV and PyramidKV are originally question-aware but are converted to a question-agnostic mock-question setting; DuoAttention is attempted but omitted from the main figure after poor performance. These choices are reasonable for the paper's one-shot compaction setting, but they complicate interpretation as general superiority over these methods.

The strongest AM variants still have nontrivial compaction overhead. Self-study query generation and OMP can require minutes on high-end GPUs, and the paper relies on an unoptimized prototype. The fastest variants are promising, but the systems claims would be stronger with integration into an actual serving stack and measurements of end-to-end latency, memory pressure, and throughput under concurrent requests.

The LongBench v2 evaluation uses a selected 47-context subset where the model is correct with full context and incorrect without context. This is useful diagnostically, but it is not a standard full-benchmark result and may overstate practical performance differences. The paper does disclose this, but broader full-set reporting would improve confidence.

Reproducibility is good at the level of algorithms and hyperparameters, but the manuscript does not clearly state whether code, compacted-cache kernels, exact benchmark splits, and generated self-study data will be released. Reproducing the full study may be expensive, particularly the Cartridges comparisons and self-study-heavy variants.

The ethical and deployment discussion is thin. KV compaction for long-running agents and clinical records can preserve and propagate sensitive context efficiently; the paper discusses instruction-following failure modes only briefly and does not deeply address privacy, data retention, or risks from more persistent long-context memory.
